Nirjhar Water Systems: What Is the Connected Module Actually Worth?

Mumbai, September 2026. Nine crore rupees, three proposals, and a board that wants to know whether the Wi-Fi chip in a water purifier earns its place.

1. The room at Andheri East

On the evening of Monday, 21 September 2026, Aditi Raghavan stayed back in the Nirjhar Water Systems office on Andheri–Kurla Road with three printouts and a deadline. The board met on Friday, 2 October, the day after Gandhi Jayanti, and it would approve the festive-quarter investment plan in that meeting. Aditi, Head of Product for the past two years, had ₹9 crore of discretionary capital to recommend against, and three proposals from three different parts of the company, each of which claimed the money.

The proposals disagreed about something more fundamental than money. Nirjhar had, fourteen months earlier, put a Wi-Fi module into its purifiers and built an app around it. The National Sales Head wanted the module taken out of the mid-tier range so that the price could come down. The Customer Success lead in Singapore wanted it extended to the company's growing commercial business. Aditi's data scientist in Toronto wanted neither, and said the company had never actually measured what the module did. By Friday, Aditi had to say which of them was right.

2. Nirjhar Water Systems

Nirjhar sold domestic water purifiers — reverse-osmosis and UV units for Indian homes — in a market defined by Eureka Forbes's Aquaguard, Hindustan Unilever's Pureit and Kent, with Livpure and a long tail of regional assemblers below them. Founded in Pune in 2014 by two former appliance engineers, the company had grown by doing two unglamorous things well: a dealer-and-installer network that covered 190 towns, and consumable filters that were cheap to make and predictable to sell. Revenue in FY26 was ₹412 crore on 3.1 lakh units, of which ₹98 crore came from filters, service contracts and spares.

In July 2025 Nirjhar had launched Nirjhar Sense: three SKUs with a Wi-Fi module, an app showing live total dissolved solids, filter life in litres rather than months, and — the commercial point of the whole exercise — automatic reordering of filters under a subscription called Nirjhar Suraksha at ₹3,900 a year, covering two filter changes and unlimited service visits. The module added ₹1,150 to the bill of materials. Connected SKUs were now 38 percent of units sold.

The team that built it was spread across time zones by accident of hiring rather than design. Firmware and cloud sat in Bengaluru; the app and the ordering backend in Pune; Lena Fischer, who had designed the onboarding flow, worked from Berlin; Nikhil Varma, the company's only data scientist, had joined from a Toronto analytics firm and stayed there; Serena Tan ran customer success from Singapore, chiefly because the company's commercial accounts in the Gulf — including Al Barsha Facilities, a Dubai firm that had bought 1,800 units for labour accommodation blocks — needed someone in a compatible time zone.

3. The situation

Two things had gone wrong in the June quarter and one thing had gone right. The wrong things came from Meenal Joshi's service operations in Pune. Returns on connected SKUs were running at 5.2 percent against 2.1 percent on the non-connected range, and service cost per unit in the first year was ₹610 against ₹430. Both were attributed, in the June review, to "teething issues with the Wi-Fi variant". The right thing came from Serena Tan: Al Barsha Facilities in Dubai had renewed and expanded, because the fleet dashboard Nirjhar had built for them in March let their maintenance team see which of 1,800 units needed a filter before a resident complained. Serena had four similar prospects in Singapore and Sharjah and no product to sell them.

In August, Nikhil Varma did the work nobody had asked for. He joined the shipment records, the installer app logs and the cloud handshake table, and found that of connected units sold through to customers in the twelve months to June 2026, only 47 percent had ever completed the pairing sequence. The 41 percent attach rate that the company had been reporting since November was computed on paired devices only. Measured against all connected units sold, subscription attach was 22 percent. Measured against all units of every kind, it was 12 percent.

Varma's second finding mattered more. Among paired devices, Suraksha attach was 41 percent. Among connected devices that had never paired, it was 12 percent — roughly the same as on the non-connected range, where the installer sold an annual maintenance contract by hand. In other words the module, on its own, appeared to be worth almost nothing. Paired, it was worth a great deal. And the returns were not evenly spread either: 71 percent of returned Sense units had never completed pairing.

Harish Kulkarni, the National Sales Head, drew the opposite conclusion from the same memo. He had been arguing since April that Kent and Livpure were winning the ₹15,999 shelf in Nagpur, Indore, Coimbatore and Lucknow, and that Nirjhar's mid-tier Sense unit at ₹17,499 was losing on price for a feature most buyers never used. Varma's data, he said, proved his point: take the module out, drop the price, win the volume, and sell the AMC the way the company always had.

4. The people

Aditi Raghavan, Head of Product, Mumbai. Two years in the role, came from a payments company, and is the only person in the building who is accountable for both the device and the app. She wants a decision the board can hold her to in twelve months, and she is aware that she has never before had to defend a hardware cost line.

Harish Kulkarni, National Sales Head, Mumbai, with a team of 240 across the country. His incentive is primary sales into the channel for the festive quarter. He wants the mid-tier module removed and the price cut to ₹15,999 before Diwali stocking, which begins on 10 October.

Meenal Joshi, Head of Service Operations, Pune, responsible for 1,400 contracted installers. She carries the warranty provision and the ₹610 per-unit service cost. She wants the connected range stabilised before it grows, and she has quietly noticed that her installers earn ₹380 for an installation and nothing for a pairing.

Serena Tan, Customer Success lead, Singapore, who owns the commercial accounts. She wants ₹2 crore of the ₹9 crore for a productised fleet dashboard, and points out that Al Barsha's 1,800 units generate more subscription revenue than 9,000 domestic units because the buyer is also the payer and the facilities team activates every unit on day one.

Nikhil Varma, data scientist, Toronto. He wants the activation sequence instrumented step by step before any money is spent, and warns that the 41-percent-versus-12-percent gap may be partly self-selection: households that pair may simply be households that were always going to buy a subscription.

Exhibit 3 was assembled by Aditi and Varma over a weekend and is the document the board will actually argue about. Its third column assumes the module is removed and the price cut by ₹1,150, with AMC attach reverting to the 11 percent the non-connected range achieves — and it also assumes, generously to Harish, that volume rises enough to hold revenue flat, which the table does not show. Its second column assumes a ₹250 pairing incentive paid on every verified pairing, including the 47 percent of pairings that happen already without being paid for, and excludes the one-time engineering and design spend that the second column depends on. 5. The options

Option A — Take the module out of the mid-tier. Drop Sense Plus to a non-connected ₹15,999 unit before Diwali stocking, keep connectivity as a Sense Pro feature only. Upside: an immediate price-competitive answer on the shelf where volume lives, a lower return rate, and ₹425 rather than ₹625 of service cost per unit. Cost: the ₹1,150 saved in BOM is nearly recovered by AMC attach falling from 28 percent to about 11 percent, and the company gives up any path to a subscription business in its largest segment. Extending the module downward instead — making it standard on the Dhaara range — would cost 1,92,200 units × ₹1,150, or ₹22.1 crore, well beyond the ₹9 crore available.

Option B — Buy activation. Spend roughly ₹5 crore on the pairing problem: a ₹250 installer incentive paid on verified pairing, a module revision with a Bluetooth fallback so the phone can bind the device without the home router, Lena's third onboarding redesign built around that fallback, and Varma's step-level instrumentation so the company can see the funnel weekly. Upside: Exhibit 3's second column, and a return rate that falls as a side effect. Of the ₹5 crore, about ₹2.6 crore is one-time — engineering, tooling, design and instrumentation — and the balance is the first year's incentive pool. Cost: the incentive is paid on every pairing, including the ones that would have happened anyway; the module revision cannot reach the 1.18 lakh units already sold; and nothing improves before January, which is after the festive quarter.

Option C — Follow the commercial money. Give Serena ₹2 crore for a productised fleet dashboard and multi-site billing, and the remaining ₹7 crore to Meenal's service network and installer training. Upside: in commercial accounts the buyer is the payer, activation is done by a maintenance team on day one, and Al Barsha's 1,800 units already prove the economics. Cost: the domestic business is 94 percent of volume and would be left exactly as it is, with 53 percent of connected units never pairing and a returns line that Meenal cannot fix by training alone.

6. Questions for discussion

1. Nirjhar has reported a 41 percent attach rate for ten months. What exactly was the denominator, what should it have been, and what decisions were taken on the strength of the wrong one?

2. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, is the connected module a failed feature or an un-activated one? What evidence would distinguish the two?

3. Varma warns that the paired-versus-unpaired attach gap may be selection rather than causation. How would you test that before Friday, and what would you do if you could not?

4. Aditi must recommend an allocation of ₹9 crore on 2 October. What does she recommend, what does she tell Harish about the Diwali shelf price, and what single metric does she offer the board as the thing she will be judged on next September?

7. A note for the learner

This case is about the five numbers that join a device business to a software business: activation, connected daily actives, attach rate, return rate and warranty or service cost per unit. Nirjhar had all five and had connected none of them. The specific failure is a denominator failure — attach computed on paired devices while being spoken about as if it applied to everything sold — and denominator failures in hardware are the norm rather than the exception, because a unit can be built, shipped, sold, registered or connected, and each is a plausible base.

A well-reasoned answer establishes three things from the exhibits before choosing. First, that the device itself is not broken: Exhibit 2's 97 percent power-on rate settles that. Second, that the module's commercial value is conditional on pairing, because attach among unpaired connected units (12 percent) is indistinguishable from the non-connected range (9 to 11 percent). Third, that the returns problem is largely the pairing problem wearing a different label — 71 percent of returned Sense units never paired, and return rate rises monotonically as pairing falls down the SKU ladder in Exhibit 1. A learner who reads the returns line as a quality defect will reach a different and defensible conclusion, but should be asked to explain why the defect is worst on the cheapest connected unit and absent on the non-connected units built in the same plant.

One defensible path: Aditi recommends Option B as the primary allocation, with a carve-out for Option C, and refuses Option A in the form Harish proposes. The reasoning is that pairing is the binding constraint on every number the board cares about — subscription revenue, returns and service cost all move with it — and that 28 points of pairing is worth about ₹4.1 lakh per thousand units on Exhibit 3 — roughly ₹4.8 crore of lifetime contribution on a single year's connected volume, recurring every year thereafter, against ₹2.6 crore of one-time engineering and a self-funding incentive pool. She takes Varma's selection warning seriously by structuring the installer incentive as a staged rollout: live in eight states from November, withheld in four comparable states until February, so that the company gets a genuine comparison instead of a correlation. She gives Serena the ₹2 crore, because commercial accounts are the one place where activation is free and the evidence already exists. And she answers Harish not with the module but with the Dhaara RO at ₹15,999, which already occupies the shelf he is worried about — while conceding that if pairing has not reached 65 percent by March, the mid-tier module should come out.

The metric she offers the board is the one the whole case turns on: thirty-day pairing rate on connected units sold through, reported weekly, owned by her. Note what that commitment implies. It is a leading metric, it is measurable without a survey, it is reachable by product work, and it is uncomfortable — because on the day she commits to it, the honest number is 47 percent.

Ojas Energy: The Module in the Carton

An Ahmedabad power-backup manufacturer has put a connectivity module into six lakh inverters. Nine-tenths of them have never spoken to the cloud. With the Diwali build plan locking in seventeen days, its chief product officer has to say what the module is worth — and every number she has been given answers a slightly different question.

1. Sunday night, Rajkot

At twenty past ten on the night of Sunday, 13 September 2026, Revathi Iyer was standing between two stacks of cartons in a distributor's godown off the Gondal Road in Rajkot, holding a torch in one hand and a printed packing list in the other. She had counted eleven returned units. Nine of them were OjasLink-enabled hybrid inverters. Seven of the nine had their app-onboarding card still sealed in its polythene sleeve, taped to the inside of the carton flap where the installer would have had to look for it.

Revathi was Chief Product Officer of Ojas Energy, and she had flown to Rajkot on Saturday morning because a set of numbers she did not believe had been circulated in a deck she was expected to defend. On Monday morning at half past nine, in the company's Ahmedabad office at Prahlad Nagar, the executive committee would lock the festive build plan: what Ojas would manufacture between the last week of September and Diwali, which fell on 8 November, and which would account for roughly 38 per cent of the company's annual domestic volume.

Item one on the agenda was a single question, phrased by Bhaskar Trivedi, the founder, in his usual manner: Does the module stay in the mid-range or not? Underneath it were three proposals, from three parts of the company, each of which had brought its own evidence and each of which was, on its own terms, correct.

The eleventh returned unit was not connected at all. It was a plain 1,100 VA inverter from the value range, two years old, with a burnt relay. Revathi had photographed it, and then stood for a while looking at the sealed onboarding cards in the other seven, and had begun to suspect that the argument the company was about to have was not really about the module.

2. How Ojas got here

Ojas Energy Private Limited was founded in 2011 in Ahmedabad by Bhaskar Trivedi, a power-electronics engineer who had spent eleven years designing sine-wave inverters for a Gujarat contract manufacturer. The company sold home power backup into a market that India's unreliable distribution network had made permanent: inverters, tubular lead-acid batteries, and from 2022 lithium-ferrophosphate packs and solar hybrid inverters for rooftop installations. FY26 revenue was ₹1,140 crore on 6.2 lakh units, of which ₹214 crore came from batteries, spares, extended warranty and service contracts. It manufactured at Sanand, employed 2,900 people, and sold through 41 distributors, about 7,800 retail counters, three national electronics chains, and — since 2021, and to the continuing discomfort of its distributors — directly on Amazon and Flipkart.

In July 2024 Ojas launched OjasLink. The idea had been Revathi's: a home inverter knows more about a household's electricity than anything else in the house, and a household that can see its backup time, its battery health and its solar generation on a phone will buy its next battery from the company that showed it. The module added Wi-Fi and Bluetooth to the inverter's control board, an app, and a paid annual service plan called Ojas Kavach at ₹2,400, covering two preventive visits, priority response and a battery health report.

One engineering decision from that launch constrains everything now. To hold the bill-of-materials adder under ₹1,000, Meghana Rao's team in Bengaluru chose a Wi-Fi-only module with no cellular fallback, no onboard storage beyond 72 hours of buffered readings, and — the consequential omission — no dedicated current-sense shunt on the battery leg. Battery state of health is therefore not measured but inferred, from voltage-recovery curves under known loads. The inference is good when the household's load profile is stable and poor when it is not. It was never validated outside Gujarat and the National Capital Region.

The second decision was commercial. Because installers, not customers, commission an inverter, Ojas paid the installing dealer ₹150 for every unit successfully paired to the app, credited monthly. It worked: dealer-channel activation ran at nearly four times the e-commerce rate within two quarters. Nobody asked, for eighteen months, whose phone the units were being paired to.

3. The industry around it

Indian home power backup is an old, crowded and unsentimental category. Luminous, Exide, Livguard, Microtek, V-Guard and Havells occupy the shelves Ojas wants, and the price ladder at every capacity point is visible to any consumer in thirty seconds on Amazon or at a Croma or Reliance Digital counter. Distributors carry three brands and push whichever pays the best margin that month. A ₹1,000 difference in the maximum retail price of a mid-range inverter is not a positioning question; it is the difference between being on the shortlist and not.

Two policy currents run underneath the market. The rooftop solar subsidy programme, PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana, has put hybrid inverters and net-metering into ordinary middle-class purchase conversations, which is good for Ojas's newest and most connected range and has brought a fresh set of installers into the channel who have never commissioned a connected device. And the tightening of BIS requirements for lithium cells and packs, alongside customs duty on imported cells, has raised the cost of exactly the products in which OjasLink is standard. The wireless module itself carries WPC and TEC obligations; the app, since the Digital Personal Data Protection Act rules came into force, carries consent and retention obligations that Ojas's legal counsel has interpreted conservatively — household load data is retained for 24 months and is not shared with dealers, which is why a dealer cannot see whether the customer he activated is actually using the app.

The global exposure is newer and noisier. In March 2025 Ojas launched a portable power-station line for the United States, sold on Amazon and run by Sameer Kulkarni from Princeton, New Jersey. The same connectivity module goes into those units. American returns behave nothing like Indian ones: the buyer returns the product, free, within thirty days, for any reason, and the leading reason code is not failure but frustration. And in the Gulf, Bayan Electrical Trading LLC of Dubai — Ojas's distributor for the UAE and Oman, run by Tarek Mansour — has been buying hybrid inverters for villa solar installations at a rate that made it, in FY26, Ojas's third-largest customer by value at ₹57 crore.

4. What happened, and what turned out not to be true

The story of the last twenty-six months can be told as three beliefs, each held sincerely and each now damaged.

The first belief was that activation meant adoption. By March 2025 Ojas was reporting 71 per cent activation on connected units sold through the dealer channel, a number that appeared in a press release and in two investor conversations. In August 2026 Anirban Dutta, the company's data scientist in Toronto, ran a duplicate-identifier audit at Revathi's request. Of the 3.41 lakh dealer-channel activations recorded since launch, 22 per cent used a mobile number that appeared on five or more activations, and 9 per cent used a number that appeared on more than twenty. Those are not households. Those are installers pairing a device to their own phone to claim ₹150, and in many cases doing so competently and in good faith, because the customer did not want to install an app while the electrician was standing in the room. Exhibit 2 sets out the funnel; the footnote is more important than the funnel.

The second belief was that connectivity paid for itself in warranty. From early 2025 the service organisation reported that connected units carried a warranty cost of ₹212 per unit against ₹389 for non-connected — a saving of ₹177, which against a module cost of ₹960 implied payback inside a battery cycle if repeat purchase was included. The number was real and the conclusion does not follow. Connected SKUs are on average nine months old; non-connected units in the field average twenty-six months, and inverter warranty claims are heavily back-loaded. Connected SKUs also sell disproportionately in metros with better power quality. And from June 2025, when the alerting system began generating pre-emptive service visits, the cost of those visits was booked to service operations rather than to warranty. Exhibit 3 carries all three caveats in its footnotes and none of them in its headline.

The third belief was that attach rate was Ojas's decision. The company sets which SKUs carry the module; it does not set what the channel stocks. Through FY26 the mid-range 1,500 VA connected SKU, priced ₹1,150 above its non-connected sibling, was steadily de-stocked by distributors in the price-sensitive markets of eastern Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and interior Maharashtra, and Yogesh Barot's team filled the gap by pushing the non-connected variant. Ojas's planned attach rate for FY26 was 64 per cent of units. The realised figure was 41 per cent, and nobody had been asked to explain the difference because no one owned the number.

A fourth thread runs alongside. Ojas Kavach, the ₹2,400 service plan, was the commercial justification for the whole programme. It has 1.19 lakh subscribers, a first-year renewal rate of 64 per cent, and gross margin of about 46 per cent after visit costs. It is also sold almost entirely to households that are genuinely using the app — which means the business case for the module rests on the 11 per cent of connected units that are active at month nine, not on the 41 per cent that shipped with it.

5. The people

Bhaskar Trivedi, founder and Managing Director, Ahmedabad. He wants a connected-services story, because a private-equity process expected to begin in the first quarter of 2027 will value recurring service revenue at a multiple the hardware business will never command. His stated position is that the module must stay in the mid-range and the company must "get activation up". What he does not say is that the ₹150 dealer bounty was his instruction, over Revathi's written objection, and that he has read the duplicate-phone audit and not circulated it.

Yogesh Barot, National Sales Head, India, Ahmedabad. Twenty-one years in the channel, and the only person in the room whom the distributors call directly. His position is that the module should come out of the mid-range immediately so that the price can drop by ₹1,150 before the festive stocking cycle, and stay only in premium and solar hybrid SKUs. His incentive is a volume-and-primary-sales target for the festive quarter. What he does not say is that three of his largest distributors have asked for a higher margin on connected units and have implied that the de-stocking would reverse if they got it.

Meghana Rao, VP Hardware Engineering, Bengaluru. Her position is that the module should become standard across the entire range, because unit economics improve at volume, because a single board simplifies manufacturing at Sanand, and because a fleet that reports its own failures is the only way Ojas will ever understand its own reliability. What she does not say is that she needs the volume to justify the redesign that adds the current-sense shunt, and that without the shunt her own battery-health readings are, in her private words to Revathi, "a good guess in Ahmedabad and a coin toss in Guwahati".

Sameer Kulkarni, VP North America, Princeton, New Jersey. His position is that connectivity is destroying the US business: the portable power stations return at 11.4 per cent, and the largest single coded reason is setup failure. He wants a hardware variant with the module omitted for the American SKUs. His incentive is a contribution-margin target that returns eat directly. What he does not say is that his team's own unboxing video, which he commissioned, shows the QR-code card falling out of the carton flap unnoticed.

Grace Lim, Director of Service Operations, Singapore. She covers distributor service for South-East Asia and the Gulf and, since a 2025 reorganisation, owns the global service P&L. Her position is that alert-driven preventive visits are the single best thing the company has built, and she has the repeat-purchase data to argue it. Her incentive is the service P&L, which is credited with Kavach revenue and charged for visits. What she does not say is that the migration of pre-emptive visit costs out of warranty and into her own line was proposed by her, for reasons she described at the time as "clean accounting".

Anirban Dutta, data scientist, Toronto. He found the duplicate phone numbers and he built the cohort decay curve in Exhibit 4. His position is that Ojas should stop reporting activation entirely and report connected units that have sent telemetry in the last 28 days, by cohort age. What he does not say is that his 28-day definition would classify as disconnected a large number of households in Bihar and Odisha whose routers are switched off during long outages — precisely the customers for whom the product matters most.

Ines Keller, principal designer, Berlin. She has argued since 2024 that the onboarding is the product and that the app is being introduced to the customer by the wrong person at the wrong moment. Her position is that Ojas should pay the installer nothing and instead trigger onboarding from the first power cut, when the household is standing in the dark looking at a working inverter. What she does not say is that this proposal has been costed at eleven weeks of engineering that would come out of Meghana's festive firmware freeze.

Tarek Mansour, Managing Partner, Bayan Electrical Trading, Dubai. Not an Ojas employee, but present in every discussion of volume. His position, stated on a call on 4 September, is that his villa-solar customers expect an app as a matter of course and that removing it from the mid-range would make Ojas uncompetitive in the Emirates against Chinese hybrid inverters. His incentive is his own installation-services business, which uses the fleet dashboard Ojas gives distributors. What he does not say is that his technicians perform most activations, and that Bayan's activation rate — 94 per cent, the highest in the company — is measured on his staff's phones.

The pre-read for Monday contains three proposals, and Revathi has spent the weekend becoming uneasy that there are three.

Option A — take the module out of the mid-range. Drop the connected variant from the 1,100 and 1,500 VA lines for the festive build, cut ₹1,150 from the shelf price, and keep OjasLink in premium, solar hybrid and Gulf SKUs only. This is Yogesh's proposal and it has the virtue of being executable in seventeen days. It halves the connected fleet's growth, cuts ₹14 crore of module cost, and concedes the mid-market to competitors at the exact moment rooftop solar is pulling ordinary households toward connected hardware. It also makes Exhibit 6's price-premium line, on which the programme's profitability depends, untestable forever.

Option B — make it standard everywhere. Meghana's proposal: fit the module to every SKU including value, absorb ₹960 on the cheapest products, and treat the fleet as infrastructure rather than as a feature. Manufacturing simplifies; unit cost falls to perhaps ₹700 at that volume; engineering gets reliability data it has never had. It requires ₹31 crore of additional working capital in a quarter that already has ₹190 crore tied up in festive stock, and it doubles down on a module whose activation Exhibit 2 shows to be partly notional and whose decay Exhibit 4 shows to be steep.

Option C — leave the hardware alone and fix activation. Kill the ₹150 dealer bounty, rebuild onboarding around Ines's first-power-cut trigger, and re-base every internal metric on 28-day telemetry rather than cumulative pairing. This costs little in cash and eleven weeks of app and firmware work that would breach the festive freeze. It also means that the connected-services numbers Bhaskar intends to show the private-equity process in January will fall — pairings of 1.90 lakh become active devices of 90,000 — before they rise.

What troubles Revathi about her own page is that all three treat the module as the subject. The eleven returns in Rajkot suggest a different subject: the installer, who is paid ₹150 for a pairing, nothing for a household that uses the app, and nothing at all for the sealed card. Grace's 4,100 preventive visits suggest another: that the thing worth measuring is not whether a device is connected but whether a household was helped before it noticed a problem. And Sameer's American returns suggest a third possibility, which nobody in the company has yet said out loud — that Ojas is running one product programme across two businesses whose customers acquire, install and abandon the product in entirely different ways, and that a single attach-rate decision for both may be the wrong shape of decision.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The build plan locks on 30 September. Long-lead components for the festive quarter — modules, magnetics, lithium cells — must be released to purchase by then, and the Sanand line changes over for the festive mix on 6 October. Any change to the board design, including Meghana's shunt, requires re-testing and fresh WPC and TEC documentation for the wireless module, which she estimates at nine to fourteen weeks; it cannot happen before Diwali under any plan.

The money is committed. ₹190 crore of working capital is already allocated to festive stock. The FY27 capital plan has ₹38 crore uncommitted, of which the finance team has provisionally earmarked ₹22 crore for a lithium pack-assembly line at Sanand. Option B needs ₹31 crore of that. The Kavach service plan carries a contractual obligation of two visits per subscriber per year to 1.19 lakh households, whatever the committee decides about new units.

The commitments to others bind hardest. Bayan Electrical Trading's annual agreement, signed in April, specifies connected hybrid SKUs for the UAE and Oman through March 2027, and Tarek Mansour has 8,400 units on order for delivery before the end of the calendar year. The DPDP consent architecture means Ojas cannot simply re-attribute installer-created app accounts to households without fresh consent from each household. And the dealer bounty, though it is a scheme and not a contract, has been announced for the festive quarter in a channel circular that went out on 1 September.

10. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibit 1, state precisely what Ojas's attach rate measures and what it does not. Whose decision does the realised 43 per cent actually reflect?

2. Exhibit 2 ranks channels one way on activation and the opposite way on what follows activation. Which definition of an activated connected product would you defend, and what does your definition make invisible?

3. Exhibit 3 appears to show that connectivity halves warranty cost. Reconstruct the three reasons it may show nothing of the kind, and describe the analysis you would run instead with the data Ojas already has.

4. Given Exhibit 4, is the right unit of measurement the device, the household, or the cohort? What would each choice do to the way the festive decision is argued on Monday?

5. Grace Lim's preventive-visit comparison is not randomised, and she says so. Sameer Kulkarni's return codes are the marketplace's, and he does not say so. How should Revathi weigh two pieces of evidence of such different quality when both point to real money?

6. It is Monday morning and the build plan locks in seventeen days. What does Revathi recommend, what does she tell the executive committee about the 1.78 lakh modules that have never reported, and what does she say in January to a private-equity buyer who has already seen the 71 per cent activation figure?

Sunday, 11.40 p.m.

The distributor's manager locked the godown and Revathi sat in the car with the door open and the packing list on her knee. She had written three lines on the back of it. The first read: 43 per cent of units carry it. The second: 15 per cent of units have used it this month. The third she had written, struck out, and written again: how many households would be worse off tonight if we removed it?

She did not know the answer to the third, and she was not sure that any system Ojas currently ran could produce it. Her phone showed a message from Bhaskar, sent forty minutes earlier: Keep it simple on Monday. One slide. Are we a connected company or not? Below it was a message from Meghana with a photograph of a board revision, and below that, unopened, one from Sameer in Princeton, where it was still Sunday afternoon.

Revathi closed the door and told the driver to go to the hotel. The seven sealed onboarding cards were in a plastic bag on the seat beside her.

Hardware and Connected-Product Metrics

For a device that phones home, the unit sold is not the story. The unit that gets switched on, stays connected, and doesn't come back in a box is.

On the second Tuesday of September 2026, Faiz Adenwala stood before Ekaant Devices' board with two numbers on the same slide, and the board could not agree on which mattered. Ekaant made NeerSense, a countertop water purifier with a companion app tracking filter life and water quality, sold through Croma, Reliance Digital, and its own site across fourteen Indian cities. The first number was hardware gross margin: 34%, ahead of budget. The second, which Faiz had added himself, was app attach rate: only 61% of the 52,000 units sold that quarter had ever been registered in the app. Nearly 20,000 purifiers sat in Indian kitchens as dumb appliances, filtering water well, generating no usage data, no filter-replacement revenue, and no warning if something failed.

Faiz was VP of Product, three years into building a connected layer atop a hardware business that had run unconnected since 2014. A growth-fund investor on the board wanted ₹40 lakh spent on an in-box voucher — free filters, redeemable only after app registration — to push attach rate toward 85%. Ekaant's finance head wanted no such thing: margin was thin, vouchers cost money, and nobody had shown a registered purifier was worth more than an unregistered one. Faiz's task that afternoon was to show, with numbers, why attach rate, activation, connected DAU, return rate, and warranty cost were one connected story about whether Ekaant was a hardware company or a hardware-enabled services company — and that the ₹40 lakh question could not be answered without knowing which.

The idea, defined plainly

Hardware and connected-product metrics are the small family of measures describing what happens to a physical product after the sale closes. Attach rate is the share of units sold that get connected to the manufacturer's digital layer within a defined window. Activation is the share of connected units whose owner completes the steps that deliver the product's core value, not merely opens an app once. Connected DAU (daily active users) counts devices or accounts exchanging meaningful data with the company's servers on a given day — hardware's version of software's daily-active-user metric. Return rate is the share of units sent back, usually within a retailer's return window, kept distinct from later churn. Warranty cost is what it costs the company, per unit or as a share of revenue, to honour repair-or-replace promises over the warranty period.

Returns and warranty cost were tracked as plain cost-accounting matters since the 1970s. What changed was connectivity: when Nest shipped its first connected thermostat in 2011, and Peloton and Kindle normalised the idea that a product's real business lived in what happened after purchase, hardware companies inherited software's vocabulary — activation, DAU, retention — and had to adapt it to objects, where a device could work perfectly and still generate zero data. The sentence Faiz could say without sounding glib: a unit sold is a transaction; a unit attached, activated, and still working is a customer — and Ekaant's filter and service revenue depended entirely on the second thing.

How it actually works

The mechanics run as a sequence, and the discipline is never letting one stage stand in for another. It starts with units sold — sell-through at retail, not units shipped to warehouses, which overstates sales by whatever sits unsold on shelves. Ekaant learned this in 2024, when "units sold" quietly meant "units shipped," making attach rate look ten points worse than it truly was.

Next comes a fixed attach window: Ekaant used 60 days from purchase, verified by matching retailer receipts against app-registration timestamps. Registrations after day 60 still counted as registrations but not toward that cohort's attach rate — otherwise the ratio would drift upward every quarter as old cohorts trickled in, flattering a number that should reflect today's onboarding experience.

Within registered units, Faiz's team defined a specific activation event — not "opened the app," which almost anyone does out of curiosity, but "completed first filter-life calibration and viewed one water-quality reading," a ninety-second sequence Ekaant's data showed was the leading indicator of six-month retention, chosen by testing three candidate events against actual retention and picking the strongest. Connected DAU then counted distinct devices syncing data on a given day, including automatic background syncs — a better signal than app opens for a passive-monitoring appliance. Return rate ran independently: units sent back within the retailer's window, unrelated to connectivity, since a customer can return a purifier the day after unboxing without ever installing the app. Conflating "didn't activate" with "returned" hides two different problems — onboarding friction versus the product itself. Warranty cost accumulated over the full two-year warranty as claims arrived, which is why finance carried an actuarial reserve rather than treating in-quarter claims as the true cost of this quarter's units.

The worked example, line by line

Ekaant's Q2 FY27 cohort: 52,000 units sold. The arithmetic below runs the base case, then a second pass where the board's ₹40 lakh voucher lifts attach rate to 85% but pulls in a less-engaged registrant mix.

Returns, tracked independently against the same 52,000 units, came to 1,560 ÷ 52,000 = 3.0%, in line with history and unrelated to attach rate. Warranty claims to date were 890 units at ₹1,340 average cost, ₹11.9 lakh against ₹1.87 crore of cohort revenue — 0.64% of revenue. But finance's actuarial model, built on three years of prior cohorts, projected roughly 2,400 eventual claims over the full two-year warranty life, putting true warranty cost near 1.7% of revenue — more than double the claims-to-date figure, purely because most of the warranty period hadn't happened yet.

The second column is the number Faiz needed the board to sit with. Spending ₹40 lakh to raise attach rate to 85% looks like an unambiguous win only if activation-of-attached holds steady. If the voucher instead pulls in price-sensitive registrants who claim it and never calibrate, activation-of-attached could fall from 72.1% to 55%, leaving activated units at 24,310 — barely above the 22,860 Ekaant already had, for ₹40 lakh spent. Attach rate is an input to the metric that matters, not the metric itself.

Eight distinctions worth holding onto

Attach rate is not activation. A customer who scans a QR code and abandons the app at the permissions prompt counts toward attach rate and nothing toward activation. When attach rate rises while activation-of-attached falls, the funnel has grown wider and shallower — a worse business dressed as a better one.

The denominator is a policy choice. Units sold, units shipped, and sell-through are three different numbers, and a team under pressure will gravitate to whichever flatters the ratio. Fix the denominator in writing before the quarter starts.

Connected DAU can hide shared devices. A purifier in a joint family kitchen might serve six people and sync from one phone. It counts devices or accounts, not humans, and per-user economics built on top of it can be badly distorted.

Return rate and churn are different failures with different owners. A return happens inside the retail window and usually indicts packaging, price, or first impression. Churn — an activated user who stops syncing months later — indicts the ongoing product. Conflating them sends the wrong team to fix the wrong problem.

Warranty cost is lagging and reserve-dependent, never finished. Any cohort still inside its warranty window understates true cost if reported as claims-to-date alone. A team without an actuarial reserve looks healthier than it is until the bill eventually arrives.

Early registrants are not representative. The first customers to attach in a quarter are disproportionately enthusiasts, with better-than-average activation and engagement. Checking attach-rate health three weeks into a quarter measures the most engaged slice, not the eventual average.

Attach rate has an infrastructure ceiling, not just a design one. In many Indian towns, home Wi-Fi is intermittent and a purifier installed by a plumber may never meet its owner's smartphone. Beyond a point, an unregistered device is not a solvable funnel problem but a customer the connected layer never reached.

None of this tells you whether the connected features were worth building. A high attach rate confirms customers can find the app; it says nothing about whether filter-life alerts justify their engineering cost against, say, a better filter. That needs willingness-to-pay or feature-level evidence, not a funnel metric.

Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and scale

In a consumer product like NeerSense, attach and activation are measured per household, and the business case is consumables revenue — a registered, activated customer was worth an estimated ₹1,900 a year in filter sales an unregistered one never generated. In B2B connected hardware — industrial sensors or fleet telematics — the unit of attachment is usually the site or fleet, not the individual device: a facilities manager onboards forty sensors at once, and attach rate becomes a story about IT procurement rather than consumer habit. In a marketplace or platform model, where a company supplies connectivity modules to other hardware brands, attach rate describes how many SDK-equipped devices across many manufacturers get registered by end consumers, and the platform often controls little of the unboxing experience that drives that number.

Scale changes the discipline more than the definitions. An early-stage company selling a few thousand units a quarter tracks warranty cost by hand, because volume doesn't yet justify an actuarial model, and a single enthusiastic retail partner can swing attach rate by several points. A company at Ekaant's scale needs the reserve-based warranty model and cohort-level funnel tracking described above, because at volume small percentage shifts represent real money, and because auditors expect a defensible methodology behind a warranty liability, not a spreadsheet.

Common mistakes

Treating attach rate as the finish line. Symptom: a dashboard reporting attach rate weekly but never activation-of-attached. Diagnostic: simply ask for the second number; if nobody can produce it quickly, that is the finding.

Comparing connected DAU across products with different natural usage cadence — daily for a fitness tracker, weekly for a purifier — as if a lower number always means worse engagement. Diagnostic: check whether the metric's window matches the product's honest usage rhythm before comparing.

Reporting warranty cost without a reserve, which understates liability for any cohort still under warranty and surfaces as a nasty surprise when an old cohort's claims spike a later quarter. Diagnostic: ask finance one question — claims-to-date, or claims-to-date-plus-reserve?

Chasing attach rate with incentives before checking where the funnel actually leaks. If activation-of-attached is already low, money aimed at registration is money aimed at the wrong leak. Diagnostic: run the funnel breakdown — "never registered" versus "registered but never activated" — before spending a rupee.

What good looks like

A well-run version of this decision starts before the board meeting. Six weeks earlier, a disciplined team would run a small controlled test — the voucher offered to a random 15% of buyers in two cities, not the whole cohort — and arrive with an actual activation-of-attached number for voucher recipients versus non-recipients, rather than an assumption. If the test showed activation holding steady, the ₹40 lakh spend is easy to defend with evidence. If it showed activation collapsing among voucher-driven registrants, the team would already know to redesign the incentive — tying it to completing calibration, not merely opening the app — before spending the full budget. Good practice here is refusing to scale a funnel intervention until its effect on the stage below it is known.

What Faiz decided

Faiz proposed a smaller, sharper test: ₹8 lakh, not ₹40 lakh, on a redesigned in-box card tying the incentive to completing calibration rather than registration alone, piloted in Pune and Ahmedabad for one quarter before any national rollout. He walked the finance head through the arithmetic showing why an 85% attach rate built on disengaged registrants could cost money rather than make it, and he committed to reporting attach rate and activation-of-attached together every quarter, never one without the other, along with a warranty-reserve estimate rather than a claims-to-date figure that understated Ekaant's real liability. The investor got his test; the finance head got her guardrail; and the board had, for the first time, a shared vocabulary for arguing about the same funnel instead of two numbers that happened to share a slide.

What Faiz needs next follows directly from where this stopped: once a device is attached and activated, its economics play out across a multi-year fleet — replacement cycles, aging failure rates, and the service revenue a large installed base can support — which is the territory of fleet and device-lifetime metrics, and of the harder question of how attach rates convert into durable service revenue rather than a one-time registration count.

Two questions worth sitting with:

If your product's attach rate rose ten points next quarter, what is the one number you would need before believing that was good news rather than an expensive illusion?

Who owns your warranty reserve assumption, and when was it last checked against whether today's cohorts still resemble the ones it was built on?

Hardware and Connected-Product Metrics

Attach rate, activation, connected DAU, return rate and warranty cost are not five dashboard tiles. They are one chain of conditional probabilities, and every link is owned by a different department.

On 14 August 2026, in a meeting room above Tarangini Motors' assembly line in Hosur, Meghna Sundaresan was asked to settle a question the company had deferred for two product cycles. Tarangini made electric two-wheelers — a ₹1,34,000 performance scooter and a ₹92,000 commuter, sold through 190 dealers and, since 2025, through Amazon.in and Flipkart. On the commuter, the telematics module was a ₹6,000 option: an eSIM, a GPS receiver and the firmware that let the scooter report rides, battery health and theft alerts. Attach rate on that option was 38%. The engineering director wanted it standard-fit on the 2027 refresh. Finance had costed the module at ₹3,100 of bill of materials and observed, correctly, that the commuter's contribution margin was ₹14,700 and could not absorb it. Meghna, VP of Product, had six weeks to produce a recommendation both would sign.

Three weeks later and 570 kilometres away, Arvind Kanitkar faced a differently shaped version of the same problem. Tushaar Cold Chain Systems, in Hyderabad, sold cellular temperature loggers to pharmaceutical distributors — a ₹4,900 device that rode inside insulated shippers and produced the continuous record that CDSCO-regulated cold-chain consignments require. Tushaar had 41,000 loggers in the field, and an attach rate of effectively 100%, because the distributor who bought the logger was the entity that deployed it. But only 63% had ever been bound in software to a route and consignment template — the step that made the record auditable rather than merely recorded. Return rate inside thirty days was 9%, and warranty cost was running at 4.1% of revenue, because loggers got packed against dry ice, crushed under vials, and occasionally shipped back frozen solid. Arvind's engineering head had proposed a sealed, non-serviceable design.

The two situations look unrelated. They are the same situation. In both, a physical object was sold, and the money the company would eventually make depended on a sequence of conditional events after the sale: the device gets connected, the connection gets used in the way that creates value, the use persists, the unit does not come back, and the unit does not fail expensively. That chain is what attach rate, activation, connected DAU, return rate and warranty cost measure — worth little as five separate tiles, and a great deal as one chain expressed in rupees per unit sold. Almost every expensive mistake in connected hardware comes from optimising one link while a different department owns the next.

The idea, and the argument it inherits

Begin with definitions, because two of these terms are genuinely ambiguous. Attach rate entered product vocabulary in the PC and console era, where it meant units of a complementary good sold per unit of the primary good: games per console, printers per PC. In that sense it is unbounded: a healthy console attach rate is six or eight. Connected hardware borrowed the word and redefined it as the share of units sold that connect to the manufacturer's digital layer within a defined window, bounded at one. Both usages are alive, and a meeting where one person means “services per device” and another “percentage registered” produces forty minutes of agreement about nothing. Activation is the share of connected units completing the event that delivers core value. Connected DAU counts devices exchanging defined data with the company on a given day. Return rate is the share of units sent back inside a channel's return window. Warranty cost is the expected cost of honouring repair-or-replace obligations across a cohort's warranty life, not the claims that happened to land this quarter.

Returns and warranty provisioning are old, audited disciplines — a durable-goods controller in 1978 would recognise both, and Ind AS 37 governs the provision. The funnel metrics are borrowed. When connected devices became ordinary, hardware firms imported software's vocabulary wholesale, and the import was not clean, because a physical product can work perfectly while generating no data at all. That asymmetry is the source of most of the disagreements below.

Three schools argue about what to do with it. The installed-base school, inherited from automotive and consumer durables, holds that the unit of account is the device across its service life: fleet size, age distribution, failure hazard, service revenue per device-year. It will sign that a device which never connects but gets serviced at a dealer is still a customer. It will not sign that an unconnected unit is a lost customer. The digital-funnel school, imported from subscription software, treats the device as an acquisition channel and measures attach, activation, cohort retention and connected DAU exactly as it would measure sign-ups. It will sign “an unconnected unit is a failed acquisition” and refuse “hardware gross margin is the business.” The contribution school, usually finance, refuses both framings: every funnel metric must convert into rupees of lifetime contribution per unit sold, net of returns and warranty, and no goal may be expressed as connected DAU. Meghna's engineering director argued from the second school and her CFO from the third, which is why more data about attach rate could not resolve it.

Mechanics: the chain, worked in rupees

Expert practice starts by writing the chain as one expression against a single denominator — units sold through to end customers, never units shipped to channel. For a unit sold, expected lifetime contribution is hardware contribution, less expected return cost, less expected warranty cost, plus the connected service contribution weighted by the probability that the unit ever becomes and stays connected. Formally, with a the attach rate, v the activation rate among attached units, s the share still connected at twelve months, m the connected margin per device-year and y the expected connected years:

C = h − (r × cr) − w + (a × v × s × m × y)

Tarangini's commuter ran as follows. Hardware contribution h was ₹14,700. Return rate r was 2.2% blended at a net cost cr of ₹5,900 once reverse logistics, refurbishment and resale write-down were counted — ₹130 per unit sold. Warranty provision w was 3.4% of ASP over three years, or ₹3,128. On the connected side, a = 0.38, v = 0.86 and s = 0.79 put the connected-and-retained share of units sold at 25.8%. Connected margin m was ₹2,450 per device-year — a ₹1,188 subscription, an insurance-partner referral fee, and paid over-the-air feature unlocks — over y = 3.1 years, about ₹7,600 per retained device. Connected contribution was therefore ₹1,961 per unit sold, and total contribution ₹13,403.

Now run the engineering director's proposal through the same expression. Standard-fit sets a to 1.0 by construction, which is precisely why attach rate stops being informative: it has been legislated. Registration and use have not. Tarangini's data from the performance variant showed v falling to 0.52 and s to 0.68 — buyers who would not have paid ₹6,000 do not pair the app just because the hardware is present. The connected-and-retained share therefore rises from 25.8% to 35.4%, worth ₹2,690 instead of ₹1,961: a gain of ₹729 per unit sold, against ₹3,100 of added bill of materials if the price does not move.

The break-evens fall out of the same arithmetic: standard-fit pays only if module cost falls below about ₹730, connected margin per device-year rises from ₹2,450 to roughly ₹10,600, or ₹2,400 of the module is carried in the retail price without denting volume.

Three steps are usually left implicit and are where teams go wrong. First the denominator: sell-through, not sell-in, fixed in writing before the quarter opens, because a team under pressure drifts toward whichever base flatters the ratio. Second the attach window — Tarangini used 45 days from vehicle registration — without which the ratio creeps upward forever as old cohorts trickle in. Third, identity: a scooter resold and re-registered appears in a naive count as a second attach against one unit sold, and Tarangini found 1,900 such duplicates — 1.2 points of overstated attach rate.

Two second-order effects deserve their own sentences. Connecting a fleet reliably raises reported warranty cost before it lowers it: when a scooter tells its owner that cell balance is drifting, complaints that would have been tolerated become claims, and Tarangini's claims rate rose 19% in the two quarters after battery diagnostics shipped while the underlying failure rate stayed flat. And the connectivity bill is itself a churn generator: when a bundled data plan expires, connected DAU falls off a cliff at exactly month twelve or twenty-four. That cliff is a billing event wearing the costume of disengagement, and more than one Indian hardware team has run a re-engagement campaign against it.

A related trap is the definition of a connected day: one fleet yields three very different curves depending on whether that means a heartbeat, a telemetry event or a human-initiated app session.

When the chain applies, and when it misleads

The framework rests on four testable conditions, each answered differently by Meghna and Arvind. First: the buyer is the user. At Tarangini, yes — the rider registers the scooter and pairs the phone. At Tushaar, no: a procurement head buys the loggers, a warehouse supervisor in Vapi deploys them, a quality manager consumes the output. Attach rate there is a procurement metric, activation a training metric, and a nudge campaign aimed at the buyer reaches nobody who touches the device.

Second: the product delivers its core value whether or not it connects. Tarangini's scooter rides perfectly as a dumb vehicle, so connection is genuinely optional and genuinely a funnel. Tushaar's logger is nothing but its record; an unbound logger is a failed product, not a disengaged user. This is where the borrowed vocabulary becomes actively misleading: when connection is constitutive of function, tracking activation as a funnel stage invites growth-style interventions for what is a reliability and field-operations problem. Arvind's 37% unbound loggers were not a persuasion failure; they were the consequence of a binding flow that required a desktop browser in a warehouse where nobody had one.

Third: a margin stream exists conditional on connection. Both pass, differently: Tarangini's is consumer subscription and referral, Tushaar's a ₹1,340 per-logger annual software fee at 62% margin. Fourth: returns are within the company's influence. Tarangini's 2.2% is dealer-mediated and fixable; much of Tushaar's 9% is spec mismatch found only after a consignment — a sales-qualification problem disguised as a returns problem.

Hard edge cases and organisational seams

Four situations break the simple chain. Multi-product. Sabal Power Tools, a Ludhiana maker of connected cordless tools, reports per-unit attach of 34% and per-customer attach of 71%: a contractor who buys nine tools registers once and pairs three. Both are correct; only the second predicts repeat purchase. Platform supply. Sindhur Connect sells connectivity modules and an SDK to appliance manufacturers. It is contractually measured on end-consumer registration rate — a number produced by unboxing experiences and retail demos it neither designs nor sees. Mature vendors negotiate that metric down to something they control, such as successful first provisioning per module shipped. Regulated devices. Umang Medtech's connected glucometer is a CDSCO-licensed device; a fall in connected DAU is not an engagement story but a potential patient-safety signal, and warranty cost sits adjacent to a recall reserve. You cannot A/B test a regulated clinical onboarding flow, so activation work there runs through design-control change requests measured in months. AI-native hardware. Tathya Vision Systems sells shelf-audit cameras to FMCG distributors; “activated” must mean the model is calibrated to that store's planogram, not that the camera is online, and each connected camera-day is at once revenue and training data.

The organisational seam is sharper than any of these. Attach rate has no natural owner: packaging belongs to operations, the in-box card to marketing, the pairing flow to the app team, SIM provisioning to hardware, the delivery demo to sales. Mature companies say they solve this with a cross-functional council. What they do is attach money to one link. Tarangini's answer was to pay dealers ₹300 per activated unit, which moved the number more in a quarter than eighteen months of meetings.

Eight distinctions that separate the expert

One word, two metrics. An expert hearing “attach rate” asks for the denominator before responding. The tell is a figure above 100%, or one person saying “get attach to 3.2” while another says “get attach to 80%.” The obvious reading — an arithmetic error — is wrong: they are using the console-era and connectivity-era definitions at once, both legitimately.

Connecting a fleet raises warranty cost first. The tell is a claims spike in the two quarters after a diagnostics feature ships, with field failure rate and return rate unmoved. The obvious reading is that the firmware broke something. The truer one is that the device now reports faults the customer previously absorbed — an experience win and a P&L hit arriving together. Budget for it before shipping, or the quality team spends a quarter chasing a defect that does not exist.

The activation event is a fitted parameter, not a definition. It should be whichever early event best predicts twelve-month retained connection, chosen by testing candidates against outcomes and re-fitted annually. The tell is a team using one activation event for three years across two app redesigns; the obvious reading, that stability preserves comparability, is wrong when the event no longer predicts anything.

Return rate is as much a channel artifact as a product signal. Tarangini's identical commuter SKU returned at 6.8% on marketplaces and 1.4% through dealers. The tell is a blended rate that moves when channel mix moves and nothing else did. The obvious reading, that online customers are fickle, misses that 30% of those returns cited pairing failure — an activation failure in the first forty-eight hours, surfacing as a return because no dealer was there to resolve it.

Connected DAU is a denominator problem wearing an engagement costume. Active devices over ever-activated, over in-warranty, over units sold: four ratios, four stories, and fleet aging quietly deflates the cumulative ones. The tell is a DAU ratio declining smoothly for six quarters with no behavioural change behind it. Devices are not disengaging; the denominator is accumulating dead units.

Device identity is fragile, and it breaks upward. Second-hand transfers, shared accounts, warranty replacements shipped with fresh serials and dealers registering demo units all inflate attach and activation. The tell is a cohort whose activation exceeds 100% of attached units, or a quarter where attach rises with no intervention behind it. Reconciling serials to sell-through records annually is dull work nobody volunteers for and everybody needs.

Warranty cost is partly a pricing decision. Extended warranty is a margin product; the cost curve is chosen, not merely suffered. The tell is warranty cost per unit falling while service-experience scores fall with it. The obvious reading is improved quality; the likelier one is that claims are being denied more often, converting a measured cost today into an unmeasured brand cost later.

Attach rate has a physical ceiling set by the installation channel. The expert's question is: who is holding a smartphone at the moment of first power-on? For a scooter delivered at a dealership, a salesperson who can be paid to help. For a logger sealed into a shipper at a warehouse dock, nobody. Past that ceiling, unregistered units are not a leak to plug with incentives; they are customers the digital layer structurally cannot reach, and the honest response is to redesign the moment, not the message.

How the practice shifts by product type and stage

In consumer hardware the chain runs per household and the money is consumables, subscription and resale value, so activation is a habit question. In B2B the unit of attachment is the site or fleet: attach is decided in procurement, activation is a field-operations outcome. In enterprise the useful metric is neither attach nor DAU but deployed-to-contracted devices at renewal. On platforms the supplier reports a number it does not control, and the mature move is contractual: measure what you own. In AI products the connected day doubles as a data-supply unit, which changes the economics of giving connectivity away.

Stage changes rigour more than definitions. Below a few thousand units, return rate is a qualitative instrument — at 200 units you call every returner — and a reserve model is false precision. At Tarangini's or Tushaar's scale, cohort discipline, a reserve struck on claims-development data and incentives attached to the correct link all become load-bearing. At maturity the numbers acquire an audience: attach rate enters investor decks, and with it the gaming pressure every externally reported number attracts. Where the difference is not real, say so: returns accounting and warranty provisioning are the same discipline everywhere. Only the funnel metrics change meaning with the product.

Three worked examples

Tushaar's sealed logger. Arvind's team modelled the design honestly and found it did not pay on the metrics it was meant to fix. Bill of materials rose ₹260 per unit. Warranty cost fell from ₹201 to ₹96, because a sealed IP67 device cannot be field-serviced badly, and returns fell from 9% to 5.5%, worth ₹22 per unit. Net: minus ₹133 per unit, about ₹80 lakh across a 60,000-unit year. The case for it lived entirely in a metric nobody had assigned to hardware: sealed loggers could ship pre-bound to a route template, lifting activation from 63% toward 88%. On 41,000 loggers that is some 10,250 additional activated devices at ₹830 of annual software margin each — ₹85 lakh a year, recurring. Marginal in year one, clearly right by year three, and visible only once activation was priced.

Sabal Power Tools, and how it failed. In 2024 Sabal set a 60% attach-rate goal and spent ₹1.1 crore buying it: register the tool in the app, receive a free two-year extended warranty. Attach rose from 22% to 67% and the goal was marked green. Then warranty cost per unit sold rose from ₹210 to ₹497, because the company had given away free precisely the expensive thing, and the tradespeople who bothered to claim it were the heaviest users with the highest failure exposure. Connected DAU per registered tool fell from 0.31 to 0.09: people registered and left. Contribution per unit sold fell ₹190 on a campaign that cost ₹1.1 crore to run.

Failure modes and their early warnings

Buying the wrong link. Warning sign: attach climbing while activation-of-attached falls inside thirty days. Diagnostic: what did this incentive cost per extra device still syncing at day 90? Cost of catching it late: a budget cycle plus, as at Sabal, a two-year warranty liability that cannot be unwound.

Cumulative-ratio reporting. Warning sign: a metric that has never once fallen. Diagnostic: show it by monthly cohort with a fixed window. Cost of catching it late: two years of strategy built on a number incapable of delivering bad news.

Claims-to-date as warranty cost. Warning sign: young cohorts reporting suspiciously low warranty percentages. Diagnostic: claims-to-date, or claims-to-date plus reserve? Cost of catching it late: a restatement, or a quarter in which three old cohorts mature at once.

Treating a reliability problem as a funnel problem. Warning sign: onboarding experiments that all come back flat. Diagnostic: of the units that never activated, how many physically could have? Cost of catching it late: a year of app work that could never have moved the number.

Where experts genuinely disagree

Should attach rate ever be a goal? For: it is the only lead measure available early enough to act on, since retention evidence arrives eighteen months late. Against: it is a proxy that is trivially gamed, and the only honest goal is contribution per unit sold. The first fails if attach interventions systematically shift registrant mix rather than behaviour, which is what Sabal demonstrated. The second fails if teams given only long-horizon financial goals stop investing in onboarding because they cannot see the feedback.

Standard-fit or optional connectivity? The standard-fit camp argues fleet value is superlinear in coverage: over-the-air updates, safety datasets, insurance partnerships and resale certification all need near-complete fleets, so a 38% fleet is worth far less than 38% of a full one. The optional camp argues that customers who pay for connectivity use it, and a ₹92,000 commuter cannot absorb ₹3,100 of hardware a quarter of buyers will never value. The disagreement is real because nobody has a credible estimate of that superlinearity at Indian mass-market price points; both sides extrapolate from Western premium vehicles.

What kind of number is warranty cost? Finance treats it as an actuarial provision, product as a leading quality indicator at SKU level, commercial as a margin product whose cost curve is deliberately chosen. All three are right about the same rupee. The dispute cannot be dissolved by picking one, only managed by reporting the provision, the SKU-level claims rate and extended-warranty attach separately, and never letting one stand in for the others.

What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this recites five metrics. Someone who has internalised it asks for the denominator before reacting to any ratio, and carries a conversion of each funnel metric into rupees per unit sold. They will not compare attach rates across channels, or activation across product generations, without saying what changed. They know which of the five numbers is a product metric and which is an accounting estimate, so they neither let the growth team argue with the controller's reserve nor let the controller set the onboarding roadmap. Above all, in a room that wants a campaign, they can say this is a reliability problem rather than a funnel problem — and then show the arithmetic.

What each of them decided

Meghna declined the binary. Standard-fit went onto the performance variant, whose ₹1,34,000 price carries ₹3,100 without strain and whose buyers activate at 86% anyway. On the commuter the module stayed optional, repriced to ₹4,500 and moved into the dealer delivery checklist, with ₹300 paid per activated unit rather than per registration. She committed Tarangini to one headline number — devices syncing at day 90 per 100 units sold — and to revisiting standard-fit when module cost fell below ₹1,400 or connected margin per device-year passed ₹4,000. Arvind approved the sealed logger, telling his board plainly that the warranty saving did not justify it and that he was buying a 25-point activation lift instead. He refused a return-rate target until the 9% had been decomposed into physical damage, specification mismatch and buyer's remorse, and moved activation off the product dashboard into field operations, where the work actually sat.

Going deeper

North Star metric — a connected product needs one metric spanning device and app; Tarangini's day-90 syncing devices per 100 units sold is exactly that.

Fleet and device-lifetime metrics — the next step once units are attached: age distribution, failure hazard, and the service revenue an installed base can carry.

Attach rates and service revenue — turns the funnel into a revenue model, where the ₹2,450-per-device-year assumption gets tested properly.

What makes a good metric — the ownership, cadence and decision test that would have caught Sabal's goal before ₹1.1 crore was spent.

Vanity vs actionable metrics — cumulative attach rate is the canonical hardware vanity metric; this keeps it off the dashboard.

GAME framework — a way to attach goals, actions, metrics and evaluation to each link in the chain rather than to its most visible end.

Acquisition, retention, monetisation actions — maps each metric to the intervention that can actually move it, so you stop applying funnel remedies to reliability faults.

Direct vs proxy, magnitude vs ratio — attach rate is a proxy expressed as a ratio, twice removed from money; this explains what that costs.

Attention, transaction, productivity games — which engagement pattern a connected product is legitimately playing, and so whether a falling app-session curve matters at all.
